tldr: By placing off-the-shelf color light sensor chips under a silicone gel, researchers built 'LuxTac'—a flexible tactile array for robot learning that resolves three-axis force at each taxel in a 3.5 mm thin profile without cameras or magnets.
hero_caption: Sensing principle of LuxTac. (a) Under normal load, the opaque black layer is indented, attenuating reflected light. (b) Under shear load, the colored silicone walls tilt, altering the color balance of light reaching the photodetector.
overview:
Tactile sensing is essential for robots to manipulate objects dexterously, but conventional tactile sensors have trade-offs. Piezoresistive designs (such as pressure-sensing films) are thin and inexpensive, but they sense only normal pressure and suffer from drift and hysteresis. On the other hand, camera-based sensors like GelSight capture shear forces and slip with high resolution, but optical depth requirements make them too bulky to tile over a gripper's fingertips or curved surfaces.

To solve this, the authors devised a clever design: placing off-the-shelf digital RGBC (red, green, blue, clear) light-to-digital converters and LEDs on a flexible PCB, topped with a silicone gel capped by an opaque black film. When pressed vertically, the light intensity drops. When pushed laterally (shear), colored silicone walls inside tilt, changing the color spectrum of the received light. Without using cameras or magnets, LuxTac provides digital three-axis force readings per taxel in a package only 3.5 mm thick.

Automated characterization on a CNC testbed showed excellent normal-force linearity ($R^2=0.999$) and a low median shear-direction error of 4.8 degrees. The authors also developed an IsaacGym-based tactile simulator matching real sensor patterns closely (cosine similarity of 0.942). In physical peg-in-hole experiments, adding tactile readings boosted the success rate from 40% to 87%. All design files and code are available as open source.
contributions: Developed a digital optical taxel array built from off-the-shelf components and a 4-layer flexible PCB, measuring roughly 3.5 mm thick and scalable to arbitrary sizes and geometries.
Introduced a gel cartridge with four-colored silicone walls between taxels that encodes three-axis force at individual taxels without cameras or magnets.
Demonstrated high linearity, low hysteresis, and strong generalization to unseen locations and contact shapes through 240 normal indentations and multi-session 3-axis shear tests.
Built an indentation-depth simulator reproducing physical contact patterns accurately, substantially improving physical manipulation success with imitation learning (ACT).

sections.heading: Can a Thin Tactile Array Capture Shear Forces Too?
sections.summary: Touch is crucial for robot learning to compensate for visual occlusions, but thin sensors typically only read pressure, while camera-based 3-axis sensors are bulky. This paper introduces LuxTac, a 3.5 mm optical taxel array resolving three-axis force at each element.
sections.details:
When a robot grasps an object, fingers occlude the contact area from external cameras, making tactile sensing vital to detect contact forces and slippage. In robot learning, thin and cheap piezoresistive arrays (e.g., Velostat) are often taped onto grippers. However, these measure only normal pressure, leaving out the shear forces essential for holding and lifting objects. Piezoresistive films also suffer from drift caused by temperature and loading history.

In contrast, camera-based optical tactile sensors like GelSight and DIGIT record high-resolution gel deformations. Yet, accommodating the camera's focal length makes them bulky, preventing them from being tiled over robot fingers.

This work turns to an array of discrete optical sensor elements (taxels). Under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, the back-scattered LED light drops monotonically with indentation depth. Because each taxel outputs independent digital data, the array can easily scale to different shapes and aspect ratios by adding more channels. Furthermore, simply swapping to a cartridge with colored silicone walls enables individual taxels to sense shear forces without modifying the underlying electronics.

sections.heading: Comparing Piezoresistive, Magnetic, and Optical Sensors
sections.summary: Tactile sensors span piezoresistive, magnetic, and camera-based optical modalities. LuxTac keeps the thin, flexible, and scalable benefits while using optical color shifts to resolve three-axis force per taxel.
sections.details:
Prior tactile arrays generally fall into three categories:

### Piezoresistive and Magnetic Arrays
Piezoresistive arrays, such as 3D-ViTac and FlexiTac, are widely used because they are thin, flexible, and easy to scale over large areas. However, material hysteresis is high, and they cannot directly measure shear forces. Magnetic skins, like ReSkin and uSkin, combine magnets and Hall-effect sensors to measure 3-axis forces, but they remain vulnerable to external magnetic fields and motor noise.

### Camera-Based and Discrete Optical Tactile Sensors
Camera-based sensors like GelSight offer high resolution, but their optical housings prevent flexible tiling. Other designs embed multiple photodiodes and LEDs without cameras (such as SpectraTac), but they often treat the whole surface deformation as a black box with neural networks, losing per-taxel modularity and scalability.

### Tactile Simulators
Robot learning requires fast simulators. While frameworks like FlexiTac require tuning spring-damper parameters to convert contact depth into force, LuxTac measures local silicone indentation directly. This allows a simple, direct mapping between geometric penetration depth in simulation and sensor outputs.

sections.heading: The 3.5 mm Secret: Color Sensors and Colored Silicone Walls
sections.summary: LuxTac mounts commercial RGBC digital light converters and LEDs on a flexible PCB topped with silicone gel. Users can hot-swap between a normal-only gel and a shear-sensing gel that encodes directional strain via color.
sections.details:
### Sensing Principle
The basic stack consists of photodetectors and LEDs on a flexible PCB, covered by a 2 mm translucent white silicone layer and capped with an opaque black film. LED light back-scatters through the white silicone to the photodetector. As the surface is indented, the black film nears the sensor, absorbing more light and monotonically reducing brightness.
In the shear cartridge (Mode 2), colored silicone walls separate adjacent taxels. Alternating red and green walls run between columns, while yellow and blue walls run between rows. Lateral shear tilts these colored walls, shifting the color balance reaching the sensor. In short, total brightness encodes indentation depth (normal force), while chromaticity shifts encode the magnitude and direction of shear.

### Electronics and Scalability
Each taxel uses an off-the-shelf, ultra-compact RGBC converter (TCS34725). Integrated 16-bit ADCs and IR-blocking filters keep signals digital right from the sensor. Because the chips share the same I2C address, they are wired through I2C multiplexers (TCA9548A) to dedicated buses and read out by a Teensy 4.1 at 100 Hz (up to ~180 Hz). Each taxel costs only about $6.30, and adding multiplexers allows tiling the array into arbitrary shapes.

### Elastomer Casting and Assembly
The gel is cast in layers using acrylic molds. Translucent white silicone (XP-565) is poured over a 0.5 mm flexible acrylic baseplate, cured, and coated with a protective black opaque film. The entire assembly is just 3.5 mm thick, conforming to flat or curved surfaces alike.

captions.F4: Hardware implementation of LuxTac. (a)(b) Flexible PCB layouts for 16- and 32-taxel configurations. (c) Readout controller board powered by a Teensy 4.1. (d) Layered assembly showing LEDs and photodetectors covered by an acrylic sheet, translucent silicone, and the black opaque film.

sections.heading: Automated CNC Tests: High Linearity and Shear Disentanglement
sections.summary: Characterization with a CNC stage and a six-axis F/T sensor showed high normal linearity and low hysteresis. With the shear cartridge, the sensor accurately predicted 3-axis forces across unseen contact locations and test sessions.
sections.details:
### Normal Force Response (Normal Cartridge)
A 4.5 mm diameter indenter performed 240 automated indentations across all taxels. Taxel-to-taxel variations due to manufacturing differences were corrected with a two-point normalization using baseline and maximum-load readings. The sensor demonstrated exceptional linearity with $R^2 = 0.999$ across a range of 0.1 N to 5.8 N. Hysteresis was low at $5.9 \pm 1.1\%$ of full scale, and repeatability error was just $2.0 \pm 0.3\%$.

### Shear Force Estimation (Shear Cartridge)
Using three indenter shapes (4.5 mm circle, 9 mm square, and 12 mm flat plate), the authors gathered data over various indentation depths and lateral displacements. A 2-layer MLP predicts per-taxel three-axis forces using features from a $3 \times 3$ taxel neighborhood (intensity change and chromaticity shifts $\Delta r, \Delta g, \Delta b$).
On held-out contact locations not seen during training, per-taxel predictions reached $R^2$ scores between 0.71 and 0.94 in $x, y, z$. For summed forces across the entire array evaluated across nine held-out sessions, the model achieved $R^2 = 0.96 / 0.96 / 0.92$ in $x/y/z$, with a median shear-direction angular error of only 4.8 degrees.

### Ablation on Chromaticity
An ablation study comparing models trained on intensity alone versus chromaticity alone confirmed that color information achieved $R^2$ values of 0.84 to 0.89 for shear forces. Red-green shifts mapped cleanly to $x$-axis forces, while yellow-blue shifts mapped to $y$-axis forces, confirming that the colored-wall design functioned as intended.

captions.F7: Three-axis force estimation with the shear cartridge. (a)(c) Per-taxel normal and shear force predictions compared to ground truth on held-out sessions. (b)(d) Array-wide summed force predictions. (e) Generalization across different indenter shapes. (f) Performance comparison using intensity alone, color alone, and both, highlighting that color information is critical for shear estimation.

sections.heading: Direct Depth Mapping Matches Sim-to-Real Contact Patterns
sections.summary: Because LuxTac measures penetration depth directly, an accurate tactile simulator was built in IsaacGym. Real-world and simulated contact patterns across four objects grasped at three angles achieved a high cosine similarity of 0.942.
sections.details:
### Simulation Setup
LuxTac was modeled in IsaacGym using the TacSL tactile framework. Conventional piezoresistive sensors require fine-tuning spring-damper parameters to match contact forces. However, LuxTac taxels inherently measure the local indentation depth $\delta_i$ of the silicone directly above them.
In simulation, the local indentation depth is sampled from the object's signed distance field (SDF) and converted into normalized signals using a calibrated depth-to-signal curve, $D_i = \alpha_i \delta^{\beta_i}$. This requires only a few fitted constants per taxel and avoids tracking LED drift.

### Sim-to-Real Alignment Verification
Four 3D-printed shapes (cuboid, cylinder, elliptical cylinder, and peg) were grasped at three orientations (horizontal, vertical, 45 degrees), yielding 12 distinct contact patterns. When running identical grasps in simulation, the cosine similarity between real and simulated 16-element vectors reached an average of 0.942 (median 0.934). Comparing mismatched objects or rotated orientations dropped the score to 0.26–0.76, confirming that geometric contact shapes are faithfully captured in simulation.

captions.F8: Comparison of physical measurements (real) and simulated readings (sim) across four objects grasped in three different orientations. Contact profiles and geometries align closely, yielding an average cosine similarity of 0.942.

sections.heading: Injecting Touch into Imitation Learning Boosts Peg Insertion
sections.summary: Using the Action Chunking Transformer (ACT), the authors trained a policy combining vision and LuxTac tactile feedback. In a peg-in-hole task, adding tactile input increased success from 40% to 87% compared to vision alone.
sections.details:
### Setup and Policy Architecture
A LuxTac sensor was attached to one finger of a robot arm (reBot Arm B601) alongside an external RGB camera. The manipulation policy used the Action Chunking Transformer (ACT). Inputs included the camera image, joint states, and the flattened 16-taxel pressure vector from LuxTac (using normal pressure readings).

### Tasks and Findings
Two tasks were evaluated:
- **Peg-in-hole**: Grasping a peg, lifting it, aligning it with a hole, and inserting it. Catching small slips and misalignments is crucial.
- **Cube sorting**: Distinguishing between smooth cubes and cubes with small raised dots, then sorting them into separate bins.

After training on 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task, the vision-only baseline succeeded in only 6 of 15 peg insertion trials (40%). Adding LuxTac tactile input raised the success rate to 13 of 15 (87%), a statistically significant improvement ($p=0.021$). Tactile feedback allowed the arm to detect subtle misalignments during grasping and adjust its trajectory accordingly.
For cube sorting, success changed marginally from 5/15 to 6/15. The current prototype's taxel pitch (~4.5 mm) was too coarse to resolve small surface dot patterns.

captions.F9: Robot experiment executions and LuxTac tactile heatmaps. In the peg-in-hole task (top), distinct contact signatures appear during grasping, hole approach, insertion, and release, directly contributing to higher policy accuracy.

sections.heading: Next Steps: Handling Small Contacts and Increasing Density
sections.summary: Because LuxTac measures deformation, the force calibration varies with contact area. Future work includes handling curved or sharp objects, incorporating shear forces into reinforcement learning policies, and increasing taxel density.
sections.details:
LuxTac measures gel deformation rather than raw contact force directly. Consequently, sharp and flat objects produce different indentation depths under the same load. The force estimation model therefore needs training on the minimum expected contact area. For robot learning, however, tracking geometric deformation directly in both simulation and the real world can be an advantage, bypassing the need for force conversion.

For the shear cartridge, embedding colored silicone walls reduced overall light sensitivity by about 27% compared to pure white gel, slightly increasing hysteresis from 5.9% to 9.1%. While current taxels cost about $6.30 each, moving to newer low-cost chips and adopting meta-learning calibrations with a few manual presses could make setup even faster.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Thin, Distributed 3-Axis Touch for Robot Learning
sections.summary: Combining off-the-shelf light converters with colored silicone gels yields LuxTac: a thin, scalable, distributed 3-axis tactile array. Its open-source hardware, simulation tools, and learning pipelines lower the barrier for tactile robot learning.
sections.details:
This paper presented LuxTac, a flexible and open-source optical taxel array. By combining independent digital color light sensor chips, LEDs, and swappable cartridges with colored silicone walls, it measures per-taxel three-axis forces in a 3.5 mm thin profile without cameras or magnets.
With high linearity, low hysteresis, and depth-based alignment in simulation, LuxTac delivered clear improvements in real-world peg insertion. With circuit schematics, firmware, casting procedures, and simulation code made open source, LuxTac offers a practical foundation for advancing tactile robot learning.

takeaways: Separates vertical depth (light attenuation) from shear direction (color shifts via tilting colored walls), enabling per-taxel 3-axis sensing in a 3.5 mm thin profile without cameras.
Every taxel features an integrated 16-bit ADC, providing noise-resistant digital outputs that scale to arbitrary layouts simply by adding I2C multiplexers.
Direct mapping between indentation depth and sensor signal enables IsaacGym simulation to match real contact patterns closely (0.942 cosine similarity) without complex contact dynamics models.
limitations: Because it estimates force from deformation, the force-to-signal response depends on object curvature and contact area; sub-taxel contacts require dedicated calibration data.
A taxel pitch of 4.4–4.8 mm is coarser than camera-based sensors (sub-millimeter), limiting its ability to distinguish fine textures like Braille or tiny bumps.
Physical robot experiments evaluated only normal pressure in the ACT policy; using per-taxel shear feedback directly in real-world policy learning remains future work.
